Balanced bike routing for everyday cycling, touring, and practical navigation. Its main strength is versatility: it avoids heavy car traffic, supports cycle routes, considers elevation, and usually produces routes that feel reasonable for normal cyclists. Its weakness is that it is not highly specialized: road cyclists may find it slower than `fastbike`, while off-road riders may find it too conservative compared with `mtb` or `gravel`. Its distinctive aspect is that it is the safest general-purpose bicycle profile and probably the best default for most users.

A trekking-bike variant that ignores cycle-route relations. Its strength is that it avoids over-prioritizing signed or mapped cycle routes when those routes are indirect, scenic, outdated, or not actually useful for the current trip. Its weakness is that it loses one of the main advantages of the normal trekking profile: following good cycling networks where they exist. Its distinctive aspect is that it answers a specific problem: "do not prefer a road just because it belongs to a cycle route."

A trekking-bike variant that avoids ferry connections. Its strength is predictability: it avoids routes that depend on ferry schedules, seasonal operation, ticketing, waiting time, or uncertain availability. Its weakness is that it may produce much longer routes in river, lake, island, or coastal regions where ferries are the practical connection. Its distinctive aspect is that it is the trekking profile for users who want land-only routing.

A trekking-bike variant that avoids steps. Its strength is practical rideability, especially for loaded touring bikes, e-bikes, cargo bikes, child trailers, or users who do not want to carry the bike. Its weakness is that it may avoid short pedestrian/cycle shortcuts and produce longer detours in cities or hilly areas. Its distinctive aspect is that it keeps the normal trekking balance but removes one of the most annoying bicycle-routing surprises: stairs.

A trekking-bike variant for routes where steeper climbs are more acceptable. Its strength is that it can choose more direct or hillier routes instead of heavily avoiding elevation. Its weakness is that it can be uncomfortable or unsuitable for casual riders, heavy bikes, trailers, or low-battery e-bike trips. Its distinctive aspect is that it keeps the trekking character but is less afraid of steep terrain than the normal trekking profile.

Optimized for fast paved cycling, racing bikes, fitness bikes, and speed-pedelecs. Its strength is speed: it prefers efficient, good-quality roads and uses a travel-time-oriented model rather than simply looking for quiet or scenic paths. Its weakness is that it can feel too road-oriented for casual riders, families, or users who strongly want low-traffic routes. Its distinctive aspect is that it is the performance-oriented bicycle profile: faster and more direct than `trekking`, but still bicycle-aware.

A fast-bike profile that gives more weight to avoiding traffic than normal `fastbike`, while still remaining performance-oriented. Its strength is that it is a good compromise for riders who want speed but do not want to be constantly routed onto busy roads. Its weakness is that it can be slightly slower or less direct than `fastbike`, and less traffic-avoidant than `fastbike-verylowtraffic`. Its distinctive aspect is that it is the middle option between pure fast routing and very traffic-sensitive fast-bike routing.

A stronger low-traffic variant for road-bike or speed-pedelec users who want to avoid cars and trucks as much as possible. Its strength is safer and calmer fast cycling, especially for solo rides, rain, night riding, or dense traffic areas. Its weakness is that it can make larger detours and may reject otherwise fast roads if they are traffic-heavy. Its distinctive aspect is that it keeps the fast-bike character but makes very-low-traffic routing the central priority.

A regional variant of `fastbike` for countries where European assumptions about trunk roads, motorways, and bicycle restrictions do not always fit. Its strength is that it can make fast-bike routing more usable in regions such as Japan, Australia, and other Asia-Pacific contexts where road classification and bicycle access may differ from Europe. Its weakness is that it is less suitable as a universal default profile. Its distinctive aspect is that it keeps the fast-bike logic but adapts the road-access assumptions for Asia-Pacific usage.

A bicycle profile focused on safer and calmer routing. Its strength is that it prioritizes avoiding unpleasant or dangerous roads more strongly than normal fast routing, making it useful for cautious riders, families, urban cycling, or users who prefer comfort over speed. Its weakness is that it can produce slower, longer, or less direct routes. Its distinctive aspect is that it is the most clearly "safety-first" bicycle option, useful when the user\'s priority is avoiding stressful traffic rather than minimizing time.

Designed for gravel bikes and mixed-surface rides. Its strength is finding routes that can include compacted gravel, tracks, and low-traffic unpaved ways while still avoiding surfaces that are too rough, muddy, steep, or slow. Its weakness is that it is not ideal for pure road bikes, because it may intentionally select unpaved sections, and it is not as trail-oriented as a true MTB profile. Its distinctive aspect is that it sits between road cycling and mountain biking: more adventurous than `fastbike`, less technical than `mtb`.

An off-road-oriented bicycle profile for mountain biking and trail-based riding. Its strength is that it can prefer paths, tracks, unpaved ways, and MTB-suitable terrain much more than normal bicycle profiles. Its weakness is that it may produce routes that are unsuitable for touring, commuting, or road bikes, especially if the user does not actually want rough paths. Its distinctive aspect is its MTB-specific behavior: it considers path preference, surface quality, smoothness, wet conditions, hill behavior, and off-road suitability.

A walking profile for hiking and mountain paths. Its strength is that it is designed around foot travel, hiking routes, path difficulty, and mountain-specific conditions instead of bicycle or car assumptions. Its weakness is that it depends heavily on good OSM tagging for paths, access, hiking routes, and difficulty levels, especially in alpine areas. Its distinctive aspect is that it is the bundled profile most clearly focused on mountain walking rather than transport efficiency.

Optimized for inline skating or similar long-distance skating activities. Its strength is surface sensitivity: it strongly prefers smooth, paved, flowing routes and avoids surfaces, barriers, traffic lights, crossings, and sharp interruptions that break skating rhythm. Its weakness is that it is very specialized and may reject routes that are acceptable for bikes or pedestrians but poor for skates. Its distinctive aspect is that it routes for skating flow, not just legal access or distance.

A minimal profile that mainly tries to minimize route distance. Its strength is simplicity: it is useful when the user explicitly wants the shortest possible accessible route or when comparing route geometry. Its weakness is that shortest is often not best: it may choose unsafe, unpleasant, steep, rough, or traffic-heavy segments. Its distinctive aspect is that it mostly ignores comfort and preference logic, making it useful as a reference profile rather than a good default.

An economical car-routing profile focused on reducing unnecessary speed, energy use, and inefficient driving patterns. Its strength is that it can prefer more energy-conscious routes instead of simply chasing the fastest road. Its weakness is that it may choose slower or less direct routes and may feel less convenient when arrival time is the main priority. Its distinctive aspect is that it is the car profile for "reasonable efficiency" rather than maximum speed.
Car, economic baseline without extra cost layer

A simplified economic car variant. Its strength is that it keeps an economy-oriented car model while reducing additional preference-based penalties, making it useful as a cleaner comparison profile. Its weakness is that it may be less refined for real navigation because it removes part of the cost logic that normally helps shape practical route quality. Its distinctive aspect is that it is best seen as a technical baseline: useful to compare with `car-eco`, less useful as the main user-facing car profile.

A car-routing profile focused on speed and travel time. Its strength is that it tends to prefer faster roads and more direct time-efficient routes. Its weakness is that it may be less economical, less quiet, less scenic, and sometimes less suitable where OSM car restrictions or local road context are incomplete. Its distinctive aspect is that it is the most obvious car profile for users who simply want to arrive quickly.
Car, fast baseline without extra cost layer

A simplified fast-car variant. Its strength is that it focuses more directly on speed-model behavior, making it useful for testing, comparison, or predictable fastest-road experiments. Its weakness is that it can be less nuanced than `car-fast`, because extra penalties and preferences are reduced. Its distinctive aspect is that it is a baseline version of fast car routing: good for technical comparison, less ideal as the default car profile.

The main flexible car profile. Its strength is adaptability: by changing parameters, it can behave more like fast car routing or more like energy-aware/eco routing. It supports preferences such as avoiding tolls, unpaved roads, motorways, and certain environments. Its weakness is that it is still simpler than a full commercial car navigation engine and depends strongly on OSM tagging quality. Its distinctive aspect is that it uses a physical/kinematic model rather than only simple road-class priorities.

A simpler car-routing variant based mainly on the kinematic speed model. Its strength is that it provides a cleaner baseline for car routing, useful for comparison, testing, or cases where extra scenic or preference-based costs should not dominate. Its weakness is that it is less expressive and less user-friendly than car-vario for normal navigation. Its distinctive aspect is that it is more of a technical baseline than a rich preference profile.

A profile for fast recumbent bikes. Its strength is that it better reflects the needs of recumbent riders than a normal road-bike profile: efficient paved roads, avoidance of bad surfaces, careful handling of elevation, and penalties for steps or dismount sections. Its weakness is that it is too specialized for normal bicycles and may avoid infrastructure that upright cyclists would accept. Its distinctive aspect is that it models a recumbent bike as its own vehicle type, not just as a faster bicycle.

A profile for fast velomobiles. Its strength is routing for very efficient, heavy, low-drag human-powered vehicles that need smooth surfaces, few stops, few obstacles, and good rolling conditions. Its weakness is that it is a poor fit for normal bicycles because it strongly penalizes narrow, rough, stop-heavy, or dismount-heavy routes. Its distinctive aspect is that it is the most vehicle-specific human-powered profile in the bundle, tuned for velomobile constraints rather than generic cycling.

A variant of `car-eco` historically linked to alternative or secondary routing data. Its strength is that it can be useful for debugging or testing car routing against a different data snapshot or special road-network preparation. Its weakness is that it is not simply a normal everyday car profile and may require special secondary-data configuration. Its distinctive aspect is that it behaves like an economic car profile but is mainly useful when the secondary-data setup is intentionally available.

An experimental profile for moped-like routing. Its strength is that it models motorized two-wheel access more naturally than a bicycle profile. Its weakness is important: it is not reliable enough for real navigation because turn restrictions and some traffic constraints may be missing. Its distinctive aspect is that it sits between bicycle and car logic, but should be treated as experimental or hidden from normal users.

A debugging profile for inspecting what OSM tags BRouter sees on route segments. Its strength is transparency: it helps developers understand the available routing data and unused tags. Its weakness is that it is not designed to produce high-quality or meaningful routes. Its distinctive aspect is that it is mainly a diagnostic profile for profile development and data inspection.

A profile for routing over railway, tram, subway, light-rail, and similar rail objects. Its strength is tracing rail network topology and checking rail connectivity in OSM data. Its weakness is that it does not represent passenger travel: no timetables, transfers, station logic, service availability, or ticketing constraints. Its distinctive aspect is that it is useful for rail-data analysis, not for normal navigation.

A profile for routing along waterways such as rivers, canals, fairways, and locks. Its strength is waterway network tracing and OSM data exploration. Its weakness is that it is too simple for real nautical navigation because it does not model boat type, depth, current, legal restrictions, hazards, or operational lock constraints. Its distinctive aspect is that it treats waterways as a routable network, but only at a basic topology level.
